## Central Limit Theorem and sampling distributions

```{=html}
<center>
<iframe src="images/clt_visualization.html" width="900" height="600"></iframe>

```

## Central Limit Theorem and sampling distributions

Under the Central Limit Theorem, we know that the sampling distribution of a sample mean is:

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
1.  Normally Distributed
2.  Centered around the population mean
3.  Has a variance of $\frac{s^2}{n-1}$ or standard error of $\sqrt{\frac{s^2}{n-1}}$
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: fragment
![](images/central_limit_theorem.webp)
:::
::::
::::::


## Sample variance

Variance of the sample mean $\bar{y}$ is:

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum^n_{i=1}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}{n-1}$$


$\bar{y}$ is the sample mean, $n$ is the sample size, and $y_i$ is a single observation.

. . .

The standard error, or the standard deviation of the *sampling distribution* of $\bar{y}$ is $\sqrt{\frac{s^2}{n-1}}$

## Sample variance

Variance of a  sample **proportion** is:

$$s^2 = {p(1-p)}$$

$p$ is the sample proportion.

. . .

The standard error, or the standard deviation of the *sampling distribution* of $\bar{y}$ is $\sqrt{\frac{s^2}{n}}$

## The distribution of sampling errors

Our knowledge of the sampling distribution is also knowledge about the distribution of sampling error.

. . .

"The sampling distribution is centered on the population mean" = "the distribution of sampling errors is centered on zero"

. . .

"The standard error of the sampling distribution is $\sqrt{\frac{s^2}{n-1}}$" = "The sampling distribution of sampling errors is $\sqrt{\frac{s^2}{n-1}}$"

## The distribution of sampling errors

The "margin of error" on a poll is the region of the sampling distribution within $\pm 1.96$ standard errors of the sample mean:

```{r}
#| fig-align: center

library(ggplot2)

# Define parameters
mean_val <- 0
sd_val <- 1
# 95% CI is roughly mean +/- 1.96 * sd
lower_bound <- qnorm(0.025, mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)
upper_bound <- qnorm(0.975, mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)

# Create the plot
ggplot(data.frame(x = c(mean_val - 4*sd_val, mean_val + 4*sd_val)), aes(x = x)) +
  # Fill the 95% area
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val),
                xlim = c(lower_bound, upper_bound),
                geom = "area", fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  # Draw the full curve
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)) +
  labs(title = "95% Filled Normal Distribution",
       subtitle = "Area within 1.96 SE of the mean",
       x = "Sample mean", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## The distribution of sampling errors

For instance, if:

-   $n = 500$
-   And the population variance is $v = 5$

. . .

Then the region within 1.96 standard errors of the sample mean is $\pm 0.196$

$SE_\bar{y} = \sqrt{5/(500-1)} \approx 0.1$

. . .

$0.1 \times 1.96 = 0.196$




## The distribution of sampling errors

We don't really test this in the real world, but we can use R to simulate it:

```{r, cache=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
set.seed(2000)
Mu <- 10 # population mean
var <- 5 # population variance
n <- 500 # sample size
sample_errors<-numeric(length = 100000) 
# 100,000 repeated samples
for(i in 1:100000){
  sample_mean<-mean(rnorm(n = n, mean = Mu, sd = sqrt(5)))
  sample_errors[i]<- sample_mean - Mu
}
# 95% of the errors are between:
quantile(sample_errors, c(.025, .975))

```

## Confidence intervals

- The margin of error - of an estimate plus or minus some expected error - is referred to in more general settings as a **confidence interval**

- Technically, a 95% confidence interval means that "95% of sample confidence intervals drawn from this same population would contain the true population parameter."

- More succinctly, a 95% confidence interval is the range of values that is *likely to contain* the true population value.


## The distribution of sampling errors: caveat

-   If the sample is sufficiently large ($\approx n\gt30$), we can estimate the population variance using the sample variance (the denominator for standard error calculations is $n-1$ to adjust for the loss of degrees of freedom from estimating the sample variance)

-   For proportions, the population variance is a function of the proportion itself, so we don't even need the $n-1$ part.

## Sampling errors and significant differences


In this context, "statistical significance" refers to the chances that two groups with the *same population mean* would have a sample mean at least as large as the one we observe in our sample.

. . .

In other words, if actual $Y_1 = Y_0$ (i.e. the population averages are equal), how often would I see a sampling error that resulted in a difference of at least $\pm 1.2$?

```{r}
#| fig-align: center

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# --- Simulate two groups ---
set.seed(42)
n <- 100
group_a <- rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 10)
group_b <- rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 10)

df <- data.frame(
  value = c(group_a, group_b),
  group = rep(c("Group A", "Group B"), each = n)
)

# --- Compute summary stats ---
stats <- df %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    mean  = mean(value),
    se    = sd(value) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# --- Run t-test ---
ttest <- t.test(value ~ group, data = df)
p_val <- ttest$p.value
p_label <- ifelse(p_val < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste0("p = ", round(p_val, 3)))

# --- Plot ---
ggplot() +
  # Jittered raw data points
  geom_jitter(
    data = df,
    aes(x = group, y = value, color = group),
    width = 0.15, alpha = 0.25, size = 1.2
  ) +
  # Shaded ±1 SE band (as a crossbar)
 # geom_crossbar(
#    data = stats,
#    aes(x = group, y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se, fill = group),
#    width = 0.25, alpha = 0.4, color = NA
#  ) +
  # Mean point
  geom_point(
    data = stats,
    aes(x = group, y = mean, color = group),
    size = 5, shape = 18
  ) +
  # Mean ± 1 SE error bar
#  geom_errorbar(
#    data = stats,
#    aes(x = group, y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se, color = group),
#    width = 0.12, linewidth = 1.2
#  ) +
  # Difference arrow + label
  annotate("segment",
    x = 1.55, xend = 1.55,
    y = stats$mean[1], yend = stats$mean[2],
    arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.08, "inches"), type = "closed"),
    color = "gray30", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 1.67, y = mean(stats$mean),
    label = paste0("Δ = ", round(diff(stats$mean), 1)),
    size = 3.5, color = "gray30"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Group A" = "#2196F3", "Group B" = "#E91E63")) +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c("Group A" = "#2196F3", "Group B" = "#E91E63")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Difference of Means Test",
    subtitle = "Diamond = mean  |  Group A SD = 10, Group B SD = 10 |  Points = individual observations",
    x = NULL, y = "Value"
    #,
   # caption  = paste0(
  #    "Two-sample Welch t-test: t(", round(ttest$parameter, 1), ") = ",
  #    round(ttest$statistic, 2), ", ", p_label
  #  )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "none",
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray50"),
    plot.caption     = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray50"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )

```

## Sampling errors and significance differences

We'll assume that the sampling distribution of the difference of means between group 1 and group 2 is 0. Now we just need to know the standard error of the difference of means.

. . .

The formula here will be slightly different depending on the scenario, but we basically just need to combine the variances of both groups:

$$\text{SE}(\bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}$$

## Sampling errors and significance differences

$$
\text{SE}(\bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}
$$ 

. . .

If $s_1^2 = 10$, $n_1=100$ and $s_2^2 = 20$, $n_2 = 100$, then:

$$ 
\text{SE}(\bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{10}{100} + \frac{20}{100}} = 0.55
$$

. . .

And now we know everything we need to know about the sampling distribution of the difference of means that we would expect if $y_1 = y_2$

## Sampling errors and significance differences

This amounts to asking "how much of the area of the normal distribution is below -1.2 or above +1.2 (the dashed lines) under a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 0.55"?

```{r}
#| fig-align: center

library(ggplot2)


# Define parameters
mean_val <- 0
sd_val <- 0.55
# 95% CI is roughly mean +/- 1.96 * sd
lower_bound <- qnorm(0.025, mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)
upper_bound <- qnorm(0.975, mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)

# Create the plot
ggplot(data.frame(x = c(mean_val - 4*sd_val, mean_val + 4*sd_val)), aes(x = x)) +
  # Fill the 95% area
  #stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val),
  #              xlim = c(lower_bound, upper_bound),
  #              geom = "area", fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  # Draw the full curve
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)) +
  labs(title = "Sampling distribution of differences at SE = 0.55",
       #subtitle = "Shading = area within 1.96 SE of the mean",
       x = "Difference of means", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1.2, lwd =.5, lty=2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.2, lwd =.5, lty=2) 


```

## Sampling errors and significance differences

Converting the value to a "Z" score allows us to use the standard normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1:
$$Z=\frac{\bar{y}_2 - \bar{y}_1}{SE_{\bar{y}_2 - \bar{y}_1}}$$

$$Z = \frac{1.2}{0.55} = 2.18$$

## Sampling errors and significance differences

We can use `pnorm` to get the area under a standard normal distribution outside of $\pm 2.18$

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# area below -2.18 SE
pnorm(-2.18, lower.tail = T)

```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# area above 2.18 SE
pnorm(2.18, lower.tail = F)

```
```{r, echo=TRUE}
# area outside of plus or minus 2.18 SE of the mean
(1-pnorm(2.18, lower.tail = T)) * 2

```
$\approx .03$ of the area

## Sampling errors and significance differences

About 1.5% of the area is to the left or right of the dashed lines. Which means about a 3% chance of seeing a sample difference at least as large as $\pm 1.2$ if the population difference is 0.

```{r}
#| fig-align: center

library(ggplot2)


# Define parameters
mean_val <- 0
sd_val <- 0.55
# 95% CI is roughly mean +/- 1.96 * sd
lower_bound <- qnorm(0.01462873, mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)
upper_bound <- qnorm(0.9853713, mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)

# Create the plot
ggplot(data.frame(x = c(mean_val - 4*sd_val, mean_val + 4*sd_val)), aes(x = x)) +
  # Fill the 95% area
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val),
                xlim = c(lower_bound, upper_bound),
                geom = "area", fill = "red", alpha = 0.6) +
  # Draw the full curve
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)) +
  labs(title = "Sampling distribution of differences at SE = 0.55",
       subtitle = "Shading = area within 2.18 SE of the mean",
       x = "Difference of means", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1.2, lwd =.5, lty=2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.2, lwd =.5, lty=2) 


```

## Sampling errors and significance differences

The probability of seeing a difference as large as the one in our sample if the actual difference is zero is a kind of **p.value**.

. . .

In more general terms, p.values reflect the probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as the one in our sample if the null hypothesis is true.

. . .

By convention, $p <.05$ is considered "statistically significant".

## Shy Trump Effect

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Phone respondents had 42% approval for Trump at a sample size of 1,778.
-   Web respondents had 44% approval for Trump at a sample size of 2,066.
-   The data are weighted, so the variances should be weighted as well ( $p(1-p)$ is very close, but not exactly the same) But this is calculated elsewhere as:
    -   $s^2_{\text{phone}} = 0.244$
    -   $s^2_{\text{web}} = 0.246$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/PM.03.30.2017_mode.effects-00-05.webp)
:::
:::::

## Shy Trump Effect

$$\bar{y}_{\text{web}} - \bar{y}_{\text{phone}} = 0.02$$

$$s^2_{\text{phone}} = 0.244; n_{\text{phone}} =1,778$$

$$s^2_{\text{web}} =  0.246; n_{\text{web}} =2,066$$

$$SE_{\bar{y}_{\text{web}} - \bar{y}_{\text{phone}}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.244}{1,778} + \frac{0.246}{2,066}} = 0.016 $$

$$\text{This difference is }\frac{0.02}{0.016} = 1.25 \text{ standard errors away from 0}$$

## Shy Trump Effect

$$\text{This difference is }\frac{0.02}{0.016} = 1.25 \text{ standard errors away from 0}$$

. . .

The p.value here is about .2:

```{r}
#| fig-align: center

library(ggplot2)


# Define parameters
mean_val <- 0
sd_val <- 0.016
# 95% CI is roughly mean +/- 1.96 * sd
lower_bound <- qnorm(0.025, mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)
upper_bound <- qnorm(0.975, mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)

# Create the plot
ggplot(data.frame(x = c(mean_val - 4*sd_val, mean_val + 4*sd_val)), aes(x = x)) +
  # Fill the 95% area
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val),
                xlim = c(lower_bound, upper_bound),
                geom = "area", fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  # Draw the full curve
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)) +
  labs(title = "Sampling distribution of differences at SE = 0.016",
       subtitle = "Shading = area within 1.96 SE of the mean",
       x = "Difference of means", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -0.02, lwd =.5, lty=2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.02, lwd =.5, lty=2) 


```

## Sampling errors and significance differences

But what about the weights!?

## Sampling errors and significance differences

The central limit theorem applies to sums, means, variances, proportions... but we're working with a weighted proportion from a stratified sample with additional adjustment for non-response. All that stuff impacts the sampling variance in complex ways.

## Sampling errors and significance differences

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
We can do these calculations ourselves in R, but for now, we can just use the **design effect** to get a rough approximation of the adjustment. The design effect is about 2.99, so...
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/deff_pew.png)
:::
:::::

## Sampling errors and significance differences

Multiplying the variance by the design effect means that there's even more random sampling error expected here.

$$SE_{\bar{y}_{\text{web}} - \bar{y}_{\text{phone}}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.244}{1,778} + \frac{0.246}{2,066}} \times \sqrt{2.99} = 0.028 $$

$$\text{This difference is }\frac{0.02}{0.028} = .71 \text{ standard errors away from 0}$$
This works out to around a p value of .4, well above the conventional threshold for significance.

## Sampling errors and significance differences

$$\text{This difference is }\frac{0.02}{0.028} = .71 \text{ standard errors away from 0}$$

Expressed as a 95% confidence interval:

$$
0.02 \pm 0.028\times 1.96 = (-0.53,0.57)
$$
Which indicates we're not really confident that the difference is positive, negative, or 0.



## Sampling errors and significance differences

- This is a "back of the envelope" calculation that loses a lot of precision due to rounding. The goal here is just to demonstrate the concept.

- We'll work on getting more precise estimates using R next week.


## Weighted mean and variance

The weighted mean ($\bar{y}_{w}$) is just the sum of each value ($y_i$) times its weight $w_i$ divided by the sum of the weights:

$$\bar{y}_{w} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i}$$

. . .

Weighted sample variance (not the variance of the sampling distribution!) is just a weighted sum of squared deviations from the mean:

$$
s^2_w = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i (y_i - \bar{y}_{w})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i}
$$
